title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 49
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Sheets from Rags
passages.text:
A. Paper is made by a process that sounds implausible until it is watched. Plant fibres are beaten in water until they separate and swell, a sieve is dipped into the resulting suspension and lifted, the water drains through leaving a mat of tangled fibres, and that mat is pressed and dried into a sheet. Nothing is added to hold it together: the fibres bond to one another as the water leaves, and the sheet's strength is a property of that bonding.

B. The raw material determined everything for most of the craft's history. The best fibres came from worn-out textiles rather than from trees, so papermaking depended on a supply of rags, and the trade in them was organised, competitive and occasionally desperate. Paper production was limited by how much cloth a society wore out, which is an unusual constraint on an industry and one that tightened as demand for printing grew.

C. Wood removed the constraint and degraded the product. Wood fibres are short, bound together with a substance that must be removed or broken down chemically, and the resulting paper is weaker and contains residues that make it acidic. Cheap paper became abundant at the moment printing volumes exploded, and the consequence was a century of books and documents that are slowly destroying themselves on the shelves.

D. That deterioration is a preservation problem of unusual shape. Material from before the change is often in better condition than material a few decades younger, because rag paper is chemically stable while acidic wood paper embrittles regardless of how carefully it is stored. Treatments exist to neutralise the acid, they must be applied item by item, and the quantity of affected material is far beyond what any programme can reach.

E. Recycling paper is more limited than its reputation suggests and worth doing anyway. Each cycle shortens the fibres, so paper cannot be recycled indefinitely and the material eventually leaves the loop as something that cannot be made into paper again; the system therefore requires continuous input of new fibre. This is a real limit and does not argue against recycling, which displaces that input several times over before the fibre is spent.

F. The predicted disappearance of paper has not occurred and the reasons are instructive. Consumption of office paper fell, packaging rose more than enough to compensate, and the properties that make paper useful — cheap, light, requiring no power, readable in any light, and usable as a physical record that cannot be silently altered — have no complete substitute. A technology can be superseded for its principal use and remain indispensable for others.

passages.title: Trees in Salt Water
passages.text:
Mangroves live where almost no other tree can, in the band between high and low tide on tropical coasts, and every feature of them is an answer to a problem that position creates. The water is salt, the mud contains almost no oxygen, the ground is unstable, and twice a day the whole arrangement is submerged and then drained. A forest growing there is solving several incompatible problems at once.

Salt is handled in two ways and most species use both. Some exclude it at the root, filtering it out of the water they take up, which requires energy and works only up to a point; others admit it and excrete it through glands in the leaves, which is why the leaves of some species are visibly salty. Both approaches make water expensive to obtain, and mangrove leaves are correspondingly thick and waterproofed like those of desert plants, which is an unexpected resemblance for a tree standing in water.

Oxygen is the more acute problem. Waterlogged mud contains essentially none, and roots need it, so mangroves grow aerial roots — projections that rise above the mud surface and admit air through pores, conducting it down to the submerged parts. The distinctive shapes people photograph are respiratory equipment, and they are why the trees can be killed by anything that raises the mud level and buries them, including sediment released by construction upstream.

The seeds solve a problem that is easy to overlook. A seed dropped into moving tidal water will usually be carried somewhere useless, so many mangroves germinate while still attached to the parent tree and drop as an established seedling that can float for a long period, remain viable, and root quickly when it grounds in a suitable place. This is unusual among trees and specific to the difficulty of establishing in a place the water is always leaving.

The services these forests provide are substantial and were valued at approximately zero for most of the period in which they were cleared. They reduce the energy of storm waves reaching the shore, they trap sediment and build land, they are the nursery habitat for a large share of coastal fish species including commercially important ones, and they store carbon in their waterlogged soils at rates per unit area among the highest of any ecosystem. Clearance for aquaculture, urban expansion and timber removed a substantial proportion of them within a few decades.

Restoration has a poor record for a reason that is well understood and frequently ignored. Planting seedlings in unsuitable places — the wrong tidal elevation, the wrong salinity, sites where the original hydrology has been altered — produces high mortality and photographs, and the projects that have worked mostly restored the water flow and let the trees return by themselves. Planting is visible and satisfying; hydrology is neither, and it is the thing that determines the outcome.

passages.title: The Copy and the Original
passages.text:
Counterfeiting is treated as a single crime and comprises at least three different problems that share only a legal category. A fake medicine with no active ingredient, a fake aircraft component that fails under load, and a fake handbag that is obviously a fake and was bought as one are not the same phenomenon, and lumping them together produces enforcement effort distributed according to which industry lobbies hardest rather than to where the harm is.

Where the buyer is deceived, the analysis is straightforward. Someone paying for a medicine and receiving chalk, or fitting a part whose certification is invented, has been defrauded and may be killed by it, and there is no interesting argument about whether this should be prevented. Substandard and falsified medicines are a substantial cause of death in regions with weak regulatory systems, and this is the part of the problem that deserves most of the attention it does not get.

Where the buyer knows, the picture is genuinely different. A person buying an obvious imitation at a fraction of the price is not a lost sale in most cases, because they would not have bought the original at its price, and the industry practice of counting each counterfeit as a lost sale produces figures that are not defensible. What the brand loses is control of its signal — the value of an expensive item that says something about its owner falls if the same appearance is available cheaply.

That signalling value is a real economic interest and an awkward one to defend in the terms usually used. The argument for protecting it is that a mark identifies a source and lets buyers rely on quality, which is sound; the argument becomes strained when the item's value is largely the mark itself and the manufacturing is comparable to that of the imitation. Enforcement in these cases protects a position rather than a customer.

Supply chains are where the serious problem actually lives, and it is not principally about handbags. Components entering legitimate manufacturing with forged certification — fasteners, semiconductors, medical devices — end up in aircraft, hospitals and infrastructure, and the failure appears long after the transaction, in a context where nobody is looking for a counterfeit. Detecting this requires auditing supply chains rather than seizing goods at borders, which is expensive and unphotogenic.

The enforcement effort is distributed almost inversely to the harm. Border seizures of consumer goods produce quantifiable statistics and press coverage; pharmaceutical verification and industrial supply-chain auditing produce neither and address the cases where people die. This is a general property of enforcement measured by activity rather than by outcome, and the counterfeit trade is a particularly clear illustration of it.
